4  A simple model of the infall

Modified

October 18, 2026

The full calculation needs a TITAN run, a spherical transfer code and 140 coupled iterations. This chapter builds a model that needs none of them, and tests each step against the full solution of Chapter 2. It has three levels:

  • the structure of the infall in closed form;
  • a closed formula for its ionization;
  • a semi-analytic version, in which the same 12-level atom sits in a prescribed radiation field, with no transfer.

Along the way it shows what actually sets the answer.

4.1 Structure in closed form

Steady free fall at \dot M onto a star of mass M and radius R:

v_{\rm ff} = \sqrt{2GM/r}, \qquad n_{\rm H}(r) = \frac{X\dot M}{4\pi r^2 v_{\rm ff}\,m_{\rm H}} = n_0\left(\frac{r}{R}\right)^{-3/2}, \qquad N_{\rm H} = 2 n_0 R\left[1 - \sqrt{R/r_{\rm out}}\right].

For \dot M = 3\,M_\odot\,{\rm yr}^{-1}, M = 10^6\,M_\odot and R = 8.4\times10^{15} cm, this gives v_{\rm ff}(R) = 1770 km s^{-1}, n_0 = 5.4\times10^8 cm^{-3} and, out to 120R, N_{\rm H} = 8.3\times10^{24} cm^{-2} [computed]. TITAN’s infall follows this free fall to within 1–2 % beyond 1.2R (Chapter 2). Fully ionized, the column has Thomson depth \sigma_{\rm T}N_{\rm H} = 5.5. Half of the column (to 120R) lies within 3.4R of the star, because N_{\rm H}(<r) \propto 1 - (R/r)^{1/2}.

Radiation trapping. An electron-scattering envelope does not absorb the star’s light, but it makes the light random-walk. Then the mean intensity exceeds the geometrically diluted value W(r)I_\nu, with W = \tfrac12[1-\sqrt{1-(R/r)^2}]. In the Eddington approximation (K = J/3) for a sphere carrying the star’s flux:

J_\nu(r) = W(r)\,I_\nu + 3H_\nu(r)\,\tau^*(r), \qquad H_\nu = \frac{L_\nu}{16\pi^2 r^2}, \qquad \tau^*(r) = r^2\int_r^\infty \frac{n_e\sigma_{\rm T}}{r'^2}\,dr' .

For n_e \propto r^{-3/2}, \tau^* = \tau_{\rm es}/5, so near the star J/J_{\rm geom} \approx 1 + 0.3\,\tau_{\rm es} \approx 2.5. In the full solution, J(\mathrm{H}\alpha)/[W B_\nu(T_{\rm eff})] is 2.0–2.5 within 2R and falls to 1.2 at 20R [computed]. A plane-parallel estimate, 1 + 1.5\,\tau_{\rm es} \approx 9, would be four times too large.

4.2 What ionizes the infall

The full solution answers this directly (julia/nlte_rates.jl) [computed]:

  • The Lyman continuum is in detailed balance. About half of all photoionizations are from the ground state, but they are balanced by recombinations to it, to 10^{-4} of all recombinations beyond 1.2R. The Lyman-continuum radiation is the infall’s own recombination light, reabsorbed nearby. That is case B, as in a nebula.
  • The net ionization comes from n = 2. Photoionization from n=2 by Balmer-continuum light exceeds recombination to n=2 by 0.10–0.35 of all recombinations, increasing outwards. This balances the recombinations to n \ge 4 that cascade down. From n=3 the net rate is small and changes sign.
  • What keeps n=2 populated is far-UV light. At 1000 Å the mean intensity in the infall is 400–1200 times that of a 7310 K blackbody, diluted.

The decisive test replaces bands of the full solution’s own J_\nu with the diluted, trapped light of a 7310 K blackbody, and recomputes the populations at fixed temperatures [computed]:

Only the far UV matters. It contains Lyα (1216 Å) and Lyβ (1026 Å): continuum light at those wavelengths pumps the optically thick Lyman lines. That fills n = 2 and n = 3, and the star’s ordinary optical light ionizes them.

Where the far UV comes from. The answer is the star itself, not the shock. The emergent spectrum of the TITAN star without any infall (star_t0) is 772 times a 7310 K blackbody at 1000 Å, 78 times at Lyα and 13 times at 1500 Å. Above the Balmer edge it is within a factor 1.2 of the blackbody [computed]. Between the Lyman and Balmer edges, a zero-metallicity photosphere without line opacity has a window: there we see deep, hot layers. With the star’s spectrum in place of the blackbody in that band, the full-J test returns a neutral column of 5.7\times10^{23} cm^{-2} [computed].

The weak point

The infall’s ionization, and with it the Hα, rests on the star’s far-UV excess. That excess comes from a photosphere computed in LTE, with continuum opacities only. The Lyman lines, Lyα above all, would absorb part of it, and metals would absorb more. Below, the far UV is reduced by up to a factor 1000 to see how much this matters.

4.3 A closed formula for the ionization

Take the three findings as assumptions:

  • the Lyman continuum is in detailed balance (case B);
  • Lyα and Lyβ are thick and in radiative balance with the star’s far UV, so n_2/n_1 = (g_2/g_1)\,J_{\rm Ly\alpha}/(2h\nu^3/c^2) and the same for n_3 with Lyβ;
  • n=2 and n=3 are photoionized by the Balmer and Paschen continua.

Both the pumping and the ionizing light scale with the same dilution-and-trapping factor f(r) = W + 3\tau^* R^2/4r^2. Ionization balance per volume, with n_e = n_p = x\,n_{\rm H}, then gives

\frac{x^2}{1-x} = \frac{f(r)^2\,Q_0}{n_{\rm H}(r)\,\alpha_B(T)}, \qquad Q_0 = \frac{g_2 I_{\rm Ly\alpha}}{g_1\,2h\nu_{\alpha}^3/c^2}\,\Gamma_2 + \frac{g_3 I_{\rm Ly\beta}}{g_1\,2h\nu_{\beta}^3/c^2}\,\Gamma_3 ,

with \Gamma_i = 4\pi\int I_\nu\sigma_i\,d\nu/h\nu the undiluted photoionization rates, all from the star’s spectrum. For the TITAN star: (g_2/g_1)I_{\rm Ly\alpha}/(2h\nu^3/c^2) = 2.7\times10^{-5}, \Gamma_2 = 1.6\times10^5 s^{-1} and \Gamma_3 = 8.0\times10^5 s^{-1}. The only other input is \alpha_B(T) (julia/closed_form.jl).

Far out, f \approx (R/2r)^2 and n_{\rm H} \propto r^{-3/2}, so the right-hand side falls as r^{-5/2}. The infall is fully ionized where it exceeds 1, and beyond, the ionized fraction falls roughly as x \propto r^{-5/4} (a little faster, since \alpha_B grows as the gas cools).

The closed form gives a neutral column of 8.8\times10^{23} against 8.0\times10^{23} cm^{-2}, and a Thomson depth of 4.98 against 5.06, on the same points [computed]. It is too ionized inside 12R and too neutral beyond 20R, by up to 0.2 in x. The profile is right to that accuracy, with no free parameter. The widget evaluates the formula live: move \dot M or the far UV and see how the ionized region responds (the temperatures stay W30’s).

4.4 The semi-analytic model

The same 12-level statistical equilibrium as the full calculation (NLTEH.solve_point), at every radius, in the prescribed field J_\nu = f(r)\,I_\nu of the TITAN star (star_t0), with case B and the \tau^* iteration, but no transfer (julia/analytic_infall.jl):

Without any transfer, the semi-analytic model gets the strong lines to 20 % and the Thomson depth to 2 %. It needs the star’s real spectrum: with a blackbody, which lacks the far-UV excess, the infall stays mostly neutral and Hα is four times weaker. Thomson trapping matters little for the lines. Lyα, which is scattered and destroyed in the infall, is where the model is worst.

How much the far UV matters. The star’s light below 1300 Å is scaled down in both models:

Hα falls only as the 0.2–0.35 power of the far UV. Even a thousandfold weaker far UV leaves it in emission, at 2\times10^{42} erg s^{-1}, and the infall still ionized (more than 95 %) within 1.6R. The strength of Hα depends on the photosphere’s far UV, but its presence does not.

4.5 Hα in closed form

In an optically thick Sobolev line the power escaping per unit volume is (4\pi\nu_0/c)(S_L - J)\langle Q\rangle, with \langle Q\rangle the angle-averaged velocity gradient. For free fall, \langle Q\rangle = (v/r)\langle|1-\tfrac32\mu^2|\rangle = 0.589\,v/r. Hence

L_{\rm line} = \frac{16\pi^2\nu_0}{c}\;0.589\int r\,v_{\rm ff}(r)\,\bigl[S_L(r) - J_\nu(r)\bigr]\,dr .

With the full solution’s S_L and J, this gives L({\rm H\alpha}) = 1.08\times10^{43} erg s^{-1}, against 1.10\times10^{43} from the exact Sobolev rates [computed]. Hα is thick everywhere it matters.

The source function falls roughly as S_L \propto r^{-1.2} out to 20R: 0.95\,B_\nu(T_{\rm eff}) at 1.2R and 0.034\,B_\nu at 20R. Beyond that it falls faster. With v_{\rm ff} \propto r^{-1/2}, the integrand goes as r^{-0.7}, so L({\rm H\alpha}) \propto r_{\rm out}^{0.3}. A factor 10 in the outer radius is a factor 2 in Hα. This is what the earlier extension test found: ending the infall at 12R instead of 120R halved the lines.

4.6 What the simple model says

  1. The infall is a Thomson-thick, partly ionized cocoon: N_{\rm H} = 2n_0R, \tau_{\rm es} \approx 5 [computed].
  2. It is ionized by the star’s own light, in two steps. The far UV pumps the Lyman lines, and the optical continuum photoionizes the excited atoms. The Lyman continuum is in case-B balance, and the shock’s X-rays do not matter [computed].
  3. A one-line formula reproduces the ionized fraction to about 0.2 and the neutral column to 10 % [computed].
  4. Hα is thick everywhere it matters. Its luminosity is an integral of r\,v\,S_L and grows slowly with the extent of the infall, as r_{\rm out}^{0.3} [computed].
  5. The weak point is the star’s far UV, which no calculation here has done with lines [interpretation].
